OGOG: GO is a new Korean cai fan stall at Bugis Junction
Image credit: OGOG: GO Bugis Junction via Google Maps
Believe it or not, I could eat cai fan every day. It’s my go-to option for a fuss-free, affordable, and yummy meal, with countless combinations to choose from. Recently, however, there’s been a surge in Korean-inspired cai png, with eateries putting a modern twist on one of the nation’s most beloved foods. OGOG: GO , a new takeaway kiosk at Bugis Junction , is one of them.
ICYMI: OGOG first debuted last year as a sit-down store at Marina One , serving homestyle Korean food with a cai fan-inspired concept, alongside gimbap and other Korean dishes. They’ve since opened four other outlets in the CBD, catering to busy lunch crowds. Enter OGOG: GO, the brand’s most recent express version of the OG dine-in concept.
Build Your Own Korean Cai Png From $9.90 At This Raffles Place Kiosk
Image credit: OGOG: GO Bugis Junction via Google Maps
The new grab-and-go outlet is located at Basement 1 of Bugis Junction, giving office-goers around the area yet another spot to dabao lunch from. There are 13 dishes to choose from, with prices starting from $8.90 , making it slightly more affordable than their sister brand.
Image credit: Veronica Lumy via Google Maps
Building a bowl here is simple, with a bowl typically comprising one base, one main, and two sides, much like a standard plate of cai fan. Start by picking your desired base. Popular picks include 18-Grain Rice , though there’s also Tofu Noodle or White Rice for something simpler.
Image credit: OGOG: GO Bugis Junction via Google Maps
Moving on to the proteins or mains. Four flavours of chicken are up for grabs, including Signature Soy , as well as Gochujang Dakgalbi and Buldak Cream for a spicy kick. The must-try here would be the Beef Bulgogi for an additional $1 . They also have Soybean Tofu for a vegetarian option.
Image credit: OGOG: GO Bugis Junction via Google Maps
Last but not least, complete your bowl with their selection of sides, featuring classic banchan such as Honey-Glazed Sweet Potatoes , Silky Steamed Egg , and Japchae . For something more unique, they also have Gochujang Broccoli and Perilla Long Beans .
That’s not all—each bowl also comes with your pick of Napa Cabbage Kimchi or Omija Pickled Radish . You also get to top your bowl off with either Gochujang Salsa or Creamy Sesame sauce.
Image credit: OGOG: GO Bugis Junction via Google Maps
If all that food isn’t enough, you can top up $3 to make your bowl a meal, which comes with a soup and a drink. For protein maxxers, add on the Oven-Baked Chicken Bites (from $4.90) , available a la carte in three sizes and two flavours: Classic Gochujang and Soy Garlic .
For more good Korean food, check out our Hanbroth coverage for Busan-style pork soup by a MasterChef Singapore Season 2 winner, or our BB.Q Chicken feature for more deets on the famous Korean fried chicken chain’s opening in Singapore.
Address: 200 Victoria Street, #B1-K06, Bugis Junction, Singapore 188201
Opening hours: Daily 11am to 9pm
Tel: 8227 8068

1-day Orchard itinerary on a budget
Orchard has always read as somewhere bougie to me, notorious for sky-high prices and luxury-brand outlets, which is probably why my friends and I tend to steer clear. After all, we don’t really have the money to splurge on a $50 meal at ION Orchard or a lavish hotel buffet .
However, after FOMO drove me down Orchard Road to admire the extravagant festive lights, I ended up putting together a full-day Orchard budget itinerary for under $30 that proves you can actually enjoy the heart of Singapore without burning a hole in your wallet.
BTW, if you’re willing to spend a little more, check out our 12-hour Orchard food itinerary instead!
How To Spend 12 Hours In Orchard: $22.80++ Porridge Buffet, $2 Thrift Stores And More
Breakfast: THE CITY BAKERY
As someone who can’t stomach a full meal during breakfast, THE CITY BAKERY is a good place to start the day with a small bite. It’s located at Mandarin Gallery , a 10-minute walk from Orchard MRT Station , offering a wide variety of pastries, bakes, and sandwiches.
ICYMI: This cafe-bakery started as a small neighbourhood bakery in New York City, founded by an ex-television producer with two Emmy Awards to his name. They’ve since expanded to Japan, with over 40 outlets at the time of writing, and recently opened their first Southeast Asian outpost in Singapore.
The bakery’s signature, and what put them on the map, is the Pretzel Croissant ($5) : a fluffy croissant with a savoury, pretzel-like crust. Inside, it’s just what you’d expect from a regular croissant—flaky with well-defined layers.
When we visited, we particularly enjoyed the Coffee Cinnamon Roll ($5) . It’s a spin on the classic breakfast pastry, zhnged up with a hit of coffee. The fragrance of the coffee brought out the earthiness and warmth of cinnamon, tying everything together.
Read our THE CITY BAKERY coverage .
Expect to spend : $5 for bakes
Address: 333A Orchard Road, #02-05 Mandarin Gallery, Singapore 238897
Opening hours: Daily 9am to 9:30pm
Website
THE CITY BAKERY is not halal-certified.
Japan-Famous Bakery Chain From NYC Opens At Mandarin Gallery—Here’s What To Try
Lunch: Maddie’s Kitchen
Image credit: Xin Hao via Google Maps
After breakfast, take some time to window-shop and soak up the atmosphere of Orchard Road before heading over to lunch at Maddie’s Kitchen in Far East Plaza . The walk from Mandarin Gallery to Far East Plaza takes about 17 minutes, which is plenty of time to jalan jalan.
Image credit: Ah Kay via Google Maps
Maddie’s Kitchen is a no-frills eatery selling affordable zi char. While most dishes are in large portions meant to be shared ‘round the table, their Hainanese Curry Rice is an item well loved by solo diners. The Pork Chop Hainanese Curry Rice ($6.80) features crispy pork cutlets served on a bed of rice, paired with a sweet-spicy Hainanese-style curry, said to be made with their house-made rempah. The set also comes with a pile of braised cabbage and a sunny-side-up fried egg, dressed with dark soya sauce.
Image credit: Glen Y via Google Maps
If deep-fried foods aren’t really your thing, their Curry Chicken Hainanese Curry Rice ($6.80) is a decent alternative, featuring the same rice and veggies, served with curried potatoes and tender chicken instead. You can also get their Braised Pork Belly Hainanese Curry Rice ($6.80) , topped with melt-in-your-mouth slices of braised pork belly.
Image credit: Snoop Ee via Google Maps
Alternatively, for something lighter, try their Batang Fish Soup or Fried Fish Soup , both priced at $7.80 . Both feature a clear, clean-tasting fish broth packed generously with a medley of ingredients: your preferred fish, tomatoes, cabbage, and silken tofu. It’s a comforting, protein-packed meal for your day’s activities.
Expect to spend : $6.80-$7.80 for mains
Address: 14 Scotts Road, #02-10/11/12/13, Far East Plaza, Singapore 228213
Opening hours: Daily 11am to 9pm
Website

Activity: Check out the events at *SCAPE
Image credit: Evelyn Yong via Google Maps
*SCAPE is one of my favourite activity spaces, and is usually chock-full of things to do. It’s a non-profit community space that supports youths’ interests in the creative arts, meaning there’s usually a wide variety of events, from arts festivals to workshops. While some require paid tickets, there are plenty of upcoming free events.
Image credit: *SCAPE
A current event running from now till 22 November 2026 is *SCAPE’s Singapore Youth Photography Awards 2026 Exhibition , which showcases the competition’s winning works, selected from over 500 submissions by a panel of distinguished judges. The collection is displayed at *SCAPE Whitespace Level 3 , free of charge. If you have an eye for photography and all things creative, take this opportunity to support Singapore’s photography talents.

Third Floor Singapore has opened on the rooftop of Design Orchard at 250 Orchard Road. It is an all-day neighbourhood bar from the team behind award-winning No Sleep Club, with cocktails, wine, coffee, food and music in a relaxed, living-room-inspired setting.
Image: Third Floor
Third Floor Singapore: a casual take on No Sleep Club
Overlooking Orchard Road, Third Floor brings the creativity and technical precision of No Sleep Club, which ranked No. 8 on Asia’s 50 Best Bars 2021 and No. 26 on The World’s 50 Best Bars 2021, into a more everyday space. Think comfortable seating, an open kitchen and bar, and a pace that suits morning coffee, casual lunches, afternoon drinks and evenings with friends.
Image: Third Floor
Founder Juan Yi Jun, who was born and raised in Singapore, says the name comes from her teenage years hanging out around Orchard. “The location became the name, and more importantly, it became ours,” she says. Her career took her through Tippling Club and Operation Dagger before she co-founded No Sleep Club.
Image: Third Floor
Cocktails worth ordering
Drinks start with a memory, an observation or a familiar ritual rather than a spirit. Jun’s graphic design training shapes how ideas are developed, with distillation, fermentation and clarification used to serve the idea, not to show off. Three drinks to look out for:
• Jolly Shandy: a beer-and-lime shandy poured over frozen house-made lime sherbet made from leftover citrus shells and peels, which you stir with a spoon.
• 3 Lime Vodka Soda: calamansi, kaffir lime leaf and Thai sweet lime with a citrus-hop distillate.
• Blue Cheese & Olive: a dirty martini with Stilton-infused gin, fino sherry, vermouth and a house-made tomato concentrate, finished with Gordal olives stuffed with blue cheese cream.
Image: Third Floor / Juan Qian
A place to return to
Beyond cocktails, Third Floor serves coffee, food, wine and beer through the day. Music and creative collaborations are part of the plan too. Events such as Void Deck Jam, which we covered when it stepped into Design Orchard on 4 October , bring DJs, independent food vendors and local collaborators together without losing the informality of a neighbourhood bar.
Image: Third Floor / Juan Qian
As Jun puts it: “We take what we do seriously, but that doesn’t mean our guests have to.”

Out with the old and in with the new — Tampines Mall has just completed its S$24 million Asset Enhancement Initiative (AEI). That’s essentially a revamp, and you can look forward to 21 new brands , refreshed retail spaces and upgraded facilities during your next visit. I believe more is more when it comes to a shopping mall, so these new shops will definitely give shoppers greater choice and a more rounded experience.
Credit – CapitaLand
Of the 21 brands introduced, 15 are new to the East. Additionally, with 14 beauty retail stores, Tampines Mall is now home to the biggest beauty cluster in the East. This includes well-known, premium brands and more accessible, everyday beauty names. The 8 new beauty brands are: CHANEL, DIOR, ELEMIS, Judydoll, Rituals, Sephora, SHISEIDO, and YSL Beauty. Besides the newbies on the block, the brands with refreshed looks are Bath & Body Works, Kiehl’s, L’Occitane, Laneige and The Body Shop.
Credit – CapitaLand
Beyond shopping until you drop, standalone boutiques on Level 1 offer distinctive personalised services . For example, SHISEIDO offers a personalised skin analysis for the best skincare and makeup recommendations.
A trip to Tampines Mall isn’t complete without having a meal; there are also 8 new F&B concepts . These dining spaces include Alchemist, Casa Vostra, Ging Sun Ho King of Bun, IM QALB by Pun Im, LONGJING, RUXU, YEAH Gelato and Charlie’s Tea. Don’t miss out on IM QALB’s Tampines Mall-exclusive menu. Plus, Charlie’s Tea’s Tampines Mall outlet is their first-ever in Singapore.
Credit – CapitaLand
Shop for a new wardrobe at 5 new fashion, sports and watch stores — Asics, Boarding Gate, Braun Buffel, Meileur Moment and CC Primos. Brands that have had a store makeover include Decathlon, Running Lab, Goldheart, SK Gold and Vincent Watch. Decathlon’s 18,000-square-foot store has more than 6,000 sporting essentials across over 60 different sports. You can try out various gear at dedicated test zones before committing to a purchase. Post-purchase services such as basic bicycle maintenance, racket restringing and re-gripping are also available.
I know where I’m heading this weekend, and I hope you do too!

Disclaimer: I’m a person who prefers strong, flavourful soups. I may not appreciate the clean, natural flavours that the brand is going for. Keep in mind that taste is subjective, so read on with a pinch of salt.
First things first: you may be wondering why there’s a disclaimer upfront, since I don’t usually do this. I just don’t think it’s fair to the brand if I dislike the food when others might enjoy it. I visited OMMA Chicken Soup at Bedok in April this year and rated it 3.5/5 , finding the soups a little too ‘clean’ and neutral for my liking. I generally prefer broths with more character and robustness.
Fast forward 7 months, and I stumbled upon Busan Pork Soup at Alexandra Village Food Centre while working on my hor fun showdown . Turns out, it’s opened by the same folks behind OMMA Chicken Soup!
Will history repeat itself, or will these soups change my mind? Let’s get to ordering!
Let me spend a moment talking about the menu. There are 4 soup bases with 3 sizes each — Tomato Busan , Double Tomato , Collagen Busan , and Kimchi Busan , with a fifth Pumpkin Busan flavour coming soon. The stall also serves Busan Torched Pork (S$3/S$4.50/S$8) as an a la carte option.
What to order at Busan Pork Soup
I spotted the words ‘Best Seller’ under the medium Tomato Busan (S$7.90) which comes with 4 pieces of sliced pork. However, I had to save tummy space and went for the small one at S$6.90 with extra Mee Sua (S$1) . The soup comes with 3 slices of pork, pig’s stomach, and sliced cabbage bathed in a light tomato broth.
Singapore’s highest-rated mutton soup stall opens for just 2.5 hours – worth the queue?
Let me first give credit to the humble mee sua , which is notoriously quick to cook and turn soggy. Thankfully, these fine strands still retained a satisfying bite, suggesting that the chef had nailed the cooking time.
Though the broth had a natural tomato flavour, much like biting into a fresh tomato, it sadly lacked sweetness, depth or even a hint of tartness. It was just… flat. Part of me wondered if this was really what a broth simmered for 10 hours was supposed to taste like. Or was its clean, neutral profile intentional, allowing customers to finish the entire bowl without feeling jelak ?
Now, let’s touch on the things that I liked. The sliced pork tasted just like a delightful, well-made cha shu that you usually find in a bowl of Japanese ramen . It was super tender, smooth, and had the perfect ratio of meat to fat. I also enjoyed the pig’s stomach pieces, which had the perfect chew and had no unpleasant odours.
I then moved on to the Collagen Broth (S$6.50 for small) and topped up S$0.80 for a bowl of Short Grain Rice . The broth comes with the same sidekicks as the Tomato Busan .
As usual, I dived straight for the broth. As with most collagen broths, the soup had a rich, viscous mouthfeel. The flavour, though (again), was far too mild, lacking any noticeable seasoning or that deep, savoury meatiness I was hoping for.
The torched pork tasted much cleaner in the collagen broth than the one from the tomato one. I tried adding the rice to the soup, and it couldn’t have been better timed, since it was pouring outside. The combination of rice and broth made for a rather heartwarming, porridge-like meal that felt especially comforting on a rainy day.
Who Busan Pork Soup is best for
If light, natural broths are what you usually go for, then the range of soups at Busan Pork Soup will surely be up your alley. But, if you’re someone like me who prefers heavier, more seasoned soups, then you’ll probably think that the flavour needs improvement.
How to get there?
Although Queenstown MRT Station (EW19) is closer to Alexandra Village Food Centre, I suggest you take the train to Commonwealth MRT station (EW20) and head to Exit B/C . There will be more bus services that will take you to these bus stops: Alexandra Ctrl and Opp Queensway Shop Ctr .
Do we recommend Busan Pork Soup?
If you’re after something light and easy on the palate after days of feasting, then yes, these soups are worth considering. I must add that the stall does the sliced pork really well. Personally, I will travel all the way here to try their Busan torched pork , but not the soup.

A shopping spree at MUJI can leave you feeling peckish, but also not wanting to spend any more than you just did. Good thing that you can get 15% off their cafe’s regular-priced a la carte dishes with a minimum of $10 spent. Their menu is on the healthier side, so you won’t have to worry about indulging in 2 pieces of their Hokkaido potato croquette. Otherwise, you can also choose from their cold deli menu’s assortment of salads. To sweeten your day further, you can also get 10% off their regular-priced clothes & household items with the same amount of minimum spend. Just remember to key in your birthdate in the Muji passport before your birth month, and you will get the discount coupon on the 10th of your birthday month.

Tucked away in an industrial estate right next to the MRT tracks in Aljunied is An La Ghien -5 , a low-key spot serving genuine, home-style Vietnamese fare from 11am all the way to 5am, making it the perfect late-night supper spot.
Founded in 2019 by Yuki, a Vietnamese immigrant in Singapore who missed the taste of home, An La Ghien -5 has since been sharing authentic Vietnamese flavours with expatriates and locals alike.
Unlike Singapore’s more commercialised Vietnamese chains, the focus here is squarely on comforting, traditional cooking. Even better, they offer a wide variety of free-flow fresh herbs to customise your meal — a Vietnamese dining touch rarely seen anywhere else on the island. I mean, look at that fridgeful of greens!
What to order at An La Ghien -5
I came here specifically for the Sliced Beef Pho (S$3.90++) . While it is a fairly standard rendition, you get a remarkably generous portion of sliced beef for the price.
The clear beef broth is clean-tasting with a subtle sweetness, paired with flat white noodles that lean slightly softer than I would prefer.
Most of the beef slices were tender, though a few pieces turned out a touch dry and firm. Tossing in the fresh herbs really helped to elevate the bowl — I went with sprigs of basil and sawtooth coriander, which added a bright, almost peppery lift to the soup.
10 best Vietnamese food places in Singapore that will blow your mind
Next I dug into the Grilled Pork Chop and Vegetables with Rice Vermicelli (S$12.90++) . This turned out to be my favourite dish here, just for how fresh and light it was, thanks to the abundance of vegetables and herbs.
The pork chop in this dish was well-seasoned and had a nice char to it, adding just a hint of smokiness. It was moist and tender throughout and wasn’t dry or tough at any point. I found it to be a little salty on its own, but when enjoyed together with the noodles and vegetables, the saltiness is just right.
The small pile of pickled water spinach added a slight tang to the bowl and paired well with the grilled pork by helping to cut through its richness.
The noodles in this dish were similarly soft, though tossing them with the crisp lettuce created a great textural contrast that made every bite much more addictive. I particularly liked the accompanying sweet chilli sauce. Infused with fish sauce, it delivered a savoury umami depth alongside a gentle spicy kick without ever leaning overly sweet.
The menu also featured less common Vietnamese dishes such as Pan-Seared Goat Ribs (S$29.90) and Fried Frog Feet with Fish Sauce (S$14.90) that I’d definitely be interested in trying next time. They also specialise in hotpot and BBQ sets, making it ideal for communal meals or family dinners.
Who is An La Ghien -5 best for?
An La Ghien -5 is ideal for anyone craving authentic, home-style Vietnamese fare. And with doors staying open until 5am, it also doubles as a perfect supper spot in the East, offering a comforting meal after hours. Plus, if you love fresh herbs, the generous free-flow spread makes it easy to customise every bowl just the way you like it.
How to get to An La Ghien -5
An La Ghien -5 is located along Lorong 23 Geylang, which is just a 2-minute walk from Aljunied MRT station (EW9) . The station connects to the East-West line of the MRT. Use Exit A and cross Aljunied Road before continuing toward Lorong 23 Geylang.
If you prefer to travel by bus, you can stop at bus stop Opp Aljunied Stn (81081) and walk towards Lorong 23 Geylang. Do note that buses 158A and 125A only operate on weekdays.
Do we recommend An La Ghien -5 ?
The free-flow herbs are a massive plus if you enjoy bright, herbaceous flavours as much as I do. Coupled with an air-conditioned dining space, it makes for a comfortable meal. While the rest of the menu is priced slightly higher than the wallet-friendly S$3.90 pho , it remains a solid spot I would likely revisit whenever I am in the area, or craving a late-night supper.

Xiao Jiao Tian, the Sichuan-inspired chain that came to Singapore by way of Fujian, is now open at Wisma Atria. It is the brand’s second outlet here, after City Square Mall in Farrer Park, and it brings the same wok-fired menu to the third floor of an Orchard Road mall.
The headline dish at both is the Bullfrog with Pickled Chilli, one of four signatures and the hottest of them, marked with two chilli symbols on the menu.
Bullfrog with Pickled Chilli, one of Xiao Jiao Tian’s four signatures. Image: Xiao Jiao Tian
Who is behind it
Xiao Jiao Tian started in Fujian Province in 2013 and grew across more than 80 kitchens in China before it crossed over. The cooking is Sichuan in spirit but softened for a wider range of palates. Several dishes come with a spice-to-taste option, which helps if one person at the table wants it hot and another does not.
The kitchen’s own rule is that every dish is cooked once it is ordered, with nothing reheated and nothing made the night before. Rice is Wuchang rice from north-east China. The brand also promises that a dish which falls short of its standard is free.
What to order
The four signatures are a good first round for two or three people:
• Bullfrog with Pickled Chilli, the spiciest of the four
• Chinese Sauerkraut Fish, sliced fish in a pickled mustard green broth, one chilli on the menu
• Honey Spicy Chicken Bites, also one chilli
• Crispy Roast Chicken, for anyone avoiding heat altogether
Chinese Sauerkraut Fish. Image: Xiao Jiao Tian
Beyond those, the best-seller section leans towards dishes that go with rice: Sizzling Beef, Golden Claypot Tofu, Steamed Pork Ribs with Rice Flour, Salted Egg Yolk Prawn and a Secret Recipe Grilled Frog. The Sweet and Sour Pork carries the Chinese name for lychee pork, the Fuzhou classic where the meat is scored so it curls up like the fruit, which is a quiet nod to where the brand began.
The full menu runs to 11 sections and more than 50 dishes, plus drinks, including a farmhouse section with Mapo Tofu and Country-Style Stir-Fried Pork, a cordyceps flower chicken soup, and shaved ices such as Golden Osmanthus Longan Ice and Fresh Fig Milk Ice. There is a separate kids’ section with crispy pork, chicken drumettes and fries, and the Steamed Egg with Minced Pork is labelled as a kids’ favourite.
Sizzling Beef, from the best-seller section. Image: Xiao Jiao Tian
The menu includes pork and pork intestines, so it is not one for halal diners.
Getting there and booking
Xiao Jiao Tian Wisma Atria is at 435 Orchard Road, #03-32/33/34, Singapore 238877. From Orchard MRT, Exit 3 leads underground into Wisma Atria at Basement 1, and the lifts go up to level three.
It opens from 11.30am to 10pm on weekdays and from 11am to 10pm on weekends, with last orders at 9pm on weekdays and 9.30pm on weekends. The hours are the same at City Square Mall, 180 Kitchener Road, #04-37.
Wisma Atria is walk-in only. Reservations are taken at City Square Mall alone, and only for groups of eight or more, on WhatsApp at +65 8099 7139 or by phone on +65 6312 4698. Delivery is through GrabFood, Foodpanda and Chinatown Delivery.

1-for-1 voco Orchard Singapore and Old Chang Kee have teamed up on Curry On! Sunday, a 1-for-1 local lunch buffet at Opus Bar and Grill every Sunday from 4 October to 29 November 2026, 12pm to 3pm. Two adults pay $108++ (about $129.50 nett, so roughly $65 each) for a full buffet with an Old Chang Kee corner of laksa-infused popiah, nasi lemak lobster kueh pie tee and curry chicken pizza, plus satay, an oyster omelette station, rock lobster laksa and a roast meat station, with free-flow coffee, tea and water. Children 6 to 12 are $28++ and under-5s eat free. The catch: the 1-for-1 is for adults 13 and up, a party must stay on one bill and one table, and it cannot be combined with other discounts or loyalty points.

The Kiri x Monchhichi collaboration is landing in Singapore, pairing bite-sized Kiri Cheesecake Cubes with collectible Monchhichi stickers. It runs from 4 November to 31 December 2026, so there is still time to collect both sets.
Image: Kiri / Bel Group
How to get the Kiri x Monchhichi stickers
The mechanic is simple. Buy any two Kiri Cheesecake Cubes or The Laughing Cow Cheez Dipper Solo at participating 7-Eleven stores, and you can redeem one free Kiri x Monchhichi sticker set. There are two sets to collect, handed out at random, so each redemption is a small surprise. Stocks are limited.
Image: Kiri / Bel Group
Stickers made for phones, laptops and water bottles
The sticker designs take their cues from the three cheesecake flavours, blending Kiri’s colourful look with Monchhichi’s nostalgic charm. They are meant to be stuck on everyday items such as laptops, notebooks, phone cases and water bottles.
Image: Kiri / Bel Group
What are Kiri Cheesecake Cubes?
Kiri Cheesecake Cubes are soft, individually wrapped cheesecake bites inspired by well-loved desserts. The flavours are Strawberry Fraisier, Raspberry Tart and Lemon Tart, and they can be eaten straight from the pack.
Image: Kiri / Bel Group
For a little more effort, the brand suggests topping a cube on a biscuit for a quick “1 Second Cheesecake”, or freezing it for a DIY ice cream pop.
Image: Kiri / Bel Group
Our take
It is an easy snack-plus-collectible offer, and the 7-Eleven redemption keeps it convenient. If you like cheese-themed Monchhichi goodies, see our earlier piece on the Laughing Cow x Monchhichi keychains , and for more convenience-store treats, check our 7-Eleven ice cream deals roundup .
Images: Kiri / Bel Group.

Sagye Lite, the casual sister of Orchard Korean pot rice restaurant Sagye, holds its grand opening at VivoCity on Wednesday 25 November with 1-for-1 sotbap for six days, to 30 November. The outlet is already in soft opening, so the doors are open now; the deal is what starts on Wednesday.
Spicy chicken with cheese sotbap at Sagye, Wheelock Place. Photo: Sagye
Sotbap is Korean rice cooked and served in its own pot, with the topping laid over the rice. At Sagye on Wheelock Place it is the centre of the menu, alongside stews and dishes to share. Sagye Lite keeps the pots and brings the prices down for everyday dining.
How the 1-for-1 works
Buy any eligible sotbap and a second eligible pot of equal or lower value is free. It is dine-in only and walk-in only, with no advance reservations for the promotion. A redemption is secured only when the order is placed in the restaurant, first come, first served.
• Lunch: 11am to 3pm, 150 redemptions
• Dinner: 5pm to 10pm, 150 redemptions
• Excluded: Signature Beef Short Rib and the F1 Japanese Wagyu Striploin sotbap
• Dates: 25 to 30 November 2026, while redemptions last
Because the free pot has to cost the same or less, two people ordering pots at the same price get the full value. Pair a cheaper pot with a dearer one and the free half of the deal is the cheaper one.
What the pots cost
Two pot prices have been shared ahead of the opening:

Makkee Dessert is a new Chinese dessert shop in Maxwell
Move over, ice cream sundaes and cakes: Chinese desserts seem to be the hot new craze. With a wave of Chinese dessert shops opening across Singapore, including Yi Man Fen and Chan Susu , Makkee Dessert is the latest to join the scene.
The space is clean and modern: think wooden furniture, light-coloured walls, and hanging paper lanterns.
The menu covers a solid range of Chinese desserts, from beloved classics including Mango Pomelo Sago ($9.80+) and Black Sesame Paste ($4.80+) to the cafe’s signature shaved ice desserts.
We tried the Mango Snow White with Black Glutinous Rice ($9.80+) , comprising milk-based shaved ice topped with fresh mango chunks, a scoop of vanilla ice cream, and a heap of black glutinous rice.
It was a pretty simple dessert: light, milky, and refreshing. The mango chunks were slightly tart, which helped to tone down some of the sweetness. The soft and stretchy glutinous rice was a good addition as well, adding some textural contrast.
If you’re a durian lover, you can opt for the Loaded Mango & Durian ($16.80+) instead. It features layers of mango- and durian-flavoured snow ice, topped with sago, grapefruit, and yam balls.
This dessert had a strong durian flavour that perfumes every bite, with the tart grapefruit cutting through some of the richness. The taro balls were QQ, while the sago pearls provided a bit of a bite. I just wished the mango flavour was more prominent, as it got lost in the mix.
What intrigued us most on the menu was the Pink Girly Vibe ($15.80+) , which we thought was a cute, kitschy name for a dessert. It features a mountain of guava-infused snow ice, topped with a dollop of cheese foam, white pearls, and a slice of guava, served on a skewer.
The snow ice had a distinct guava flavour but it was slightly gritty. While the dollop of cheese foam on top was rich, creamy, and tasty on its own, the snow ice and cheese foam didn’t really work well together. The white pearls were a fun addition, though, adding a satisfying pop with every bite.
Image credit: 林林 via Google Maps
We were bummed that the cafe ran out of their trendy rice mochi desserts during our visit. Their Pistachio Rice Mochi ($9.80+) is highly raved about online, featuring warm, nutty pistachio paste topped with a dollop of soft, stretchy rice mochi, then finished with a sprinkle of toasted pistachio.
Makkee Dessert is located opposite to Maxwell MRT Station .

The name comes from what Koreans say when they clink glasses. The whole concept is built on juansang, the Korean custom of serving food specifically to go with drinks, so the dishes are meant to sit alongside a glass rather than compete with it.
Image credit: JJAN
Executive Chef Yoo Gwangsoo runs the kitchen. Before Saint Pierre, he worked at Jean-Georges in Dubai and at Lab XXIV in Seoul and Busan. At JJAN, he applies French techniques to Korean drinking food and uses some local produce.
Image credit: JJAN
Makgeolli is the main draw here, and the rotating list covers more than the sweet, milky bottles you’d find at the supermarket. Expect light, fresh brews, thicker and stronger takju, naturally sparkling versions, and unpasteurised saeng makgeolli. Saeng makgeolli still has live yeast and spoils quickly, so it needs an unbroken cold chain and rarely makes it to Singapore. Founder Lee Haedong visited breweries across Korea to pick the labels, and many are new to Singapore.
Image credit: JJAN
There are also clear rice liquors, yakju, and cheongju. They look a lot like sake but are fermented with nuruk, a traditional Korean starter, which gives them their own aromas. Top picks to look out for include the golden Midam Seoktanju ($19++) , whose name roughly means “a wine too good to swallow”, and the drier Suamju ($18++) , which has melon and Korean pear notes.
The wine list leans towards bottles from Korean winemakers working in France, including Burgundy’s Lou Dumont.
Image credit: JJAN
Every meal starts with two house-made table snacks: a crisp sesame jeonbyeong cracker and prawn chips dusted with chilli salt.

Image credit: JJAN

Bigger spenders can go for the charcoal-finished Wagyu Beef Tongue ($58++) with bayam, a leafy vegetable also known as amaranth.

The 41-seat shophouse has a hanok-inspired interior with a painted dancheong ceiling, carved wooden brackets, and furniture made by craftsmen in Korea. It’s a six-minute walk from Maxwell and Tanjong Pagar MRT Stations .

Most of us grew up eating local fare. Over the years, we’ve grown so accustomed to the default ingredients that make up each dish that hanging one or two elements might seem like a mortal sin to purists. Take for example, nasi lemak , which is always paired with an open-faced omelette and chicken wings. So, when I found out through Google Reviews that Warmhouse Nasi Lemak at Chinatown Complex makes a couple of tweaks to this classic dish, curiosity got the better of me, and I had to swing by to try it for myself.
When we arrived, the inspiration behind the word ‘warmhouse’ became apparent. A quaint ceiling lamp cast a warm orange glow over the space, making it feel as though we had stepped into the kitchen of a welcoming household, awaiting for a humble home-cooked meal to be served.
We met Kenneth, a Singaporean ex-photographer, together with his ex-makeup artist wife, Cindy, a Taiwanese from Kaohsiung. Cindy shared that Kenneth enjoys cooking and loves to eat, while she’s obsessed over nasi lemak . Together, the couple decided to experience what it’s like to be a hawker and made the decision to combine the essences of both countries into their plates of nasi lemak . It also reminds them of their daughter, who is also a blend of 2 cultures.
What to order at Warmhouse Nasi Lemak
I fondly remember my first trip to Taiwan, where my ex-interns from my previous job had brought me to a pushcart stall near their university in Kaohsiung. An elderly uncle sold an assortment of deep-fried goodies, and that was where I first discovered my love for salt and pepper fried snacks. One bite, and I was hooked!
Thus, I was excited when we started off with the Set B Taiwanese Salt & Pepper Popcorn Chicken Nasi Lemak (S$5.50) — yes, I know, what a mouthful. I must say, for S$5.50 , to have at least 8 to 9 pieces of popcorn chicken was more than worth the price. They were accompanied by the usual peanut-anchovies combo, a fried onsen egg, sambal , and sliced Japanese cucumbers.
If you’re wondering whether this is the usual supermarket-bought frozen chicken nonsense, think again. Kenneth painstakingly marinates, breads, and deep-fries fresh chicken from scratch. As my molars sank into each crispy morsel, I was greeted by an almost-scalding gush of natural juices, accompanied by fragrant breading seasoned with salt, pepper, and five-spice powder, plus crispy fried basil leaves. Man, was it shiok !
Instead of the usual omelette or fried sunny-side up, the couple serves the dish with a lightly-fried whole ramen egg. I mean, who on earth would have thought that a flowy ramen egg would go so impeccably well with nasi lemak ? Soft, oozy, and melt-in-the-mouth — it was the perfect pairing. Cindy said the reason why they use ajitama eggs was because she dislikes how hard an omelette can get especially when it becomes cold.
The house-made sambal deserves a shout-out, too. Beyond its sweetness, it had a gritty texture and strong notes of sauteed onions and dried shrimp that gave it plenty of character. Mix copious amounts into the rice and thank me later!
Speaking of which, the rice wasn’t forgettable either, boasting a fluffy texture and rich coconut fragrance. I’m rarely blown away by every single component of a dish, but this was one of those rare occasions when everything just clicked with my palate.
We then moved on to the Set A Warmhouse Nasi Lemak (S$5) , which looked more like the default presentation that you see at almost every kopitiam or hawker centre stall. It came with a fried chicken wing, luncheon meat, and the same partners in crime as the previous dish.
The chicken wing was executed well, crispy and still maintained its juiciness. It also was seasoned properly — both skin and flesh — something that many other establishments fail to do. I’m rather icky whenever the skin and outer layer is flavourful, but the meat turns out bland and boring. It just goes to show that many of them didn’t marinate it long enough for the seasoning to penetrate thoroughly. As someone who drastically cut down on processed foods, that piece of luncheon meat felt like a little guilty pleasure. Simple, comforting, and thoroughly satisfying, it tasted like my childhood.
Who Warmhouse Nasi Lemak is best for
It’s perfect for nasi lemak traditionalists who love their default combinations. However, I’d recommend bringing a friend or two along so you can order one each to share, giving you the opportunity to savour both the traditional and more unique fusion versions.
How to get there?
You can take the MRT and alight at either Chinatown MRT Station (NE4/DT19) or Maxwell MRT Station (TE18) . Alternatively, there are bus services bringing you to the nearest bus stops: Maxwell Stn Exit 2 and New Bridge Ctr .

Tan Ser Seng Herbal Soup , the Geylang shop that has sold turtle soup since 1946, has opened its first mall outlet at Great World this month, in the year the family business turns 80.
The new restaurant sits at #B1-106/107, 1 Kim Seng Promenade. It opens daily from 11am to 10pm, with last order at 9.30pm, and closes only for Chinese New Year. Great World MRT on the Thomson-East Coast Line (TE15) is the easy way in: Exit 6 leads into the mall at Basement 2, and the restaurant is one floor up.
Claypot Turtle Soup, the house signature since 1986. Photo: Tan Ser Seng Herbal Soup
From a shoulder pole to Lorong Bachok
The family traces its roots to Fengtang Xiang in Chao’an. Tan Ah Sai arrived in Singapore in 1927, aged 11, and after the war cooked herbal turtle soup for workers rebuilding the city, selling it bowl by bowl from a shoulder-pole pushcart before saving for a tricycle. He founded the business in 1946.
His son Tan Khar Seng took over the fire in 1973, at 20, while supporting eight siblings, and his wife Tay Ah Lek cooked through the night. In 1986 the shop moved to individual claypots, which the family bills as Singapore’s first claypot turtle soup. It settled at 29 Lorong Bachok in 1992, and the third generation, Vivian and Allan, joined in the 2000s.
The Tan family, photographed in a Singapore studio in the 1960s. Photo: Tan Ser Seng Herbal Soup
What a bowl costs
The family publishes dine-in prices for the Geylang shop and has not posted a separate Great World menu, so treat these as the reference point rather than a promise for Kim Seng Promenade.
• Claypot Turtle Soup: S$28 small, S$50 medium, S$78 large
• Double Boiled Turtle Soup: S$16 small, S$21 medium
• Premier Fish Maw and Abalone Soup: S$30
• Ginseng Black Chicken Soup and Cordyceps Chicken Soup: S$15 each
• Sugarcane, Water Chestnut and Imperatae Root Soup: S$9.90
The double-boiled small bowl is the cheapest way into the turtle soups. Sides run from S$6 for cucumber in vinaigrette to S$16.90 for steamed seabass with Teochew olive vegetable, and a bowl of Fragrant Yam Rice is S$2.50. The menu does not state whether service charge or GST applies. Prices on GrabFood, foodpanda and Oddle run higher than in the shop.
Double Boiled Turtle Soup, from S$16 at the Geylang shop. Photo: Tan Ser Seng Herbal Soup
Cordyceps Chicken Soup, S$15 at the Geylang shop. Photo: Tan Ser Seng Herbal Soup
Before you go
There are no table reservations at either branch. Seating is walk-in, first come, first served. The Great World outlet takes WhatsApp messages only, on 8997 0368. Pick-up orders and food reservations go through a separate WhatsApp line, 8737 2929, and food is set aside once paid.
Tan Ser Seng is not halal-certified. It serves pork dishes, and some soups carry a splash of house herbal wine. The family describes its soups in traditional terms and is clear that the descriptions are not medical advice.
The original shop at 29 Lorong Bachok keeps shorter hours, 11am to 8.30pm daily with last order at 8pm, a five-minute walk from Aljunied MRT.

Growing up, one of my favourite desserts has always been old-school waffles —the kind you get from under-HDB bakeries. 10 Best Old-School Waffles Ranked, Filled With Biscoff Spread, Sea Salt Caramel And More

This humble waffle stall is run by 35-year-old Yu Shu Fen, who used to work as a pastry chef for well-known bakeries and cafes, including the likes of Dimbulah Coffee. With her education in Pastry & Baking at ITE College West and years of experience in the industry, she was well on her way to becoming a sous pastry chef.
However, things took a turn when she became the main caregiver of her elderly mother after her father passed away from a stroke back in 2023. Needing more time and flexibility, she quit her job and decided to start Take A Bre in 2025, selling waffles and Hong Kong-style egglets.
Image credit: T greensake via Google Maps
The shift was not easy at first, having to juggle low footfall and the many expenses of running a F&B business. Slowly, the shop started gaining traction online for both Shu Fen’s perseverance and, of course, her delicious waffles.
With more exposure, Take A Bre is now known as an up-and-coming waffle store, offering more than 20 flavours to choose from.
Image credit: Brandon Lim
Unlike most heartland bakeries, their waffles boast a crispier exterior and soft centre, and are served with generous filling. It’s definitely thicker and more hearty than the old-school waffles we’re used to. Shu Fen also makes her own batter from scratch, with a recipe she developed after much trial and error.
Image credit: John Tan via Google Maps
Their best-selling flavour would be Nutella ($3.50) , followed by the Biscoff ($4) and Banana Nutella ($4.50) . Another contender would be the Kaya & Butter ($3.50) , where the waffle is slathered in copious amounts of kaya and served with thicc slabs of butter.
Image credit: X L via Google Maps

Image credit: Denise L via Google Maps
If sweets ain’t your thing, their savoury options look just as enticing, with lesser-seen flavours such as Truffle ($5) and Chicken Floss & Mayo ($5) . Purists can opt for their Plain/Kosong waffle ($2.50) , which is also the cheapest item on the menu.

Tokyo’s iconic dessert sensation, Mr. CHEESECAKE , is officially debuting in Singapore with an exclusive pop-up at ION Orchard from 11 Nov to 30 Dec 2026 . Founded by acclaimed Chef Koji Tamura, the cheesecake brand has achieved legendary status — selling over 1 million whole cakes globally.
Prior to establishing Mr. CHEESECAKE, Chef Tamura built a distinguished career at world-renowned fine-dining establishments, including Mirazur and Restaurant ES in France. He also served as head chef at Tokyo’s TIRPSE, which is famous for receiving a Michelin star in the shortest time in the world.
Despite his impressive resume, Chef Tamura was most inspired by childhood memories of his mother’s home-baked treats and his own experience of baking a cake for a high school friend’s birthday. He began crafting cheesecakes late at night and sharing them on social media. The overwhelming online response eventually led him to depart from fine-dining kitchens and launch Mr. CHEESECAKE.
What sets Mr. CHEESECAKE apart from other cheesecake brands is its signature dual-layer construction that consists of a delicately baked top layer paired with a velvety, near-rare bottom layer. This unique construction is deliberate, allowing the flavours, aroma and mouthfeel of the cake to evolve with temperature changes and provide different sensory experiences with the same cake:
Frozen: Enjoyed straight from the freezer for a refreshing, ice-cream-like bite.
Half-Thawed (1–1.5 hours): Offers a dual texture with a frozen centre wrapped in a creamy outer coat.
Fully Thawed: Unlocks rich sweetness and aroma with a silky consistency akin to creme brulee.
We got to sample Mr. CHEESECAKE Matcha (S$69) , RICH TIRAMISU (S$69) and Mr. CHEESECAKE Sakekasu Coconut (S$69), served fully thawed. Do note that cakes are only sold whole and portions pictured in my article are tasting samples.
My favourite cake by far was Mr. CHEESECAKE Sakekasu Coconut , which carried sweet and floral tropical notes. This unusual combination pairs sake kasu with rich coconut and uplifts it with a touch of lychee puree. The sake kasu , which is the leftover pressed lees from sake production, brings a mildly yeasty and tangy flavour — akin to yoghurt — to the cake.
This gentle acidity pairs well with the smooth, buttery profile of the coconut and pleasant floral aroma of lychee, making for a complex and layered profile with depth without feeling too heavy or sweet.
Another offering that I thoroughly enjoyed was Mr. CHEESECAKE Matcha (S$69) . It might be too intensely earthy for casual drinkers like me, but dedicated matcha lovers are bound to adore it. It also features light, creamy mascarpone and a dash of vanilla to balance the richness and slight bitterness of the matcha. Despite the bold flavours of this cake, it remains remarkably light and enjoyable with just the right level of sweetness.
Finally, we moved on to the RICH TIRAMISU (S$69). Rather than a purely traditional tiramisu, Mr. CHEESECAKE’s version incorporates Japanese ingredients like hojicha , which imparted an earthy, roasted aroma.
Building on that roasted aroma, the addition of browned butter lends more depth and a slight nuttiness to the overall profile. In the middle sits a thin, crisp almond dacquoise layer to provide a textural variation from the mousse-like interior. However, for a tiramisu, I found it rather lacking in coffee flavours.
Driven by Chef Tamura’s humble ethos — “Not the world’s best, but we make your days the best” — this limited-time pop-up brings one of Japan’s most coveted pastries to local dessert enthusiasts. Make sure to head down between 11 Nov and 30 Dec 2026 to get a taste of his renowned cheesecakes.

Chai Chuan Tou Yang Rou Tang is a Chinese-style mutton soup stall at 115 Bukit Merah View Food Centre , with eager customers already forming a queue before it even opens for the day. Erm, well, not quite for the whole day. It operates for just 2.5 hours (11am – 1.30pm) , 5 days a week . With a rating of 4.6 stars out of 5 with a total of 369 reviews (at time of writing), it’s Singapore’s highest-rated mutton soup stall on Google Reviews .
A little voice in my head went, “It must be pretty darn good, eh?” This stall has also been awarded a Michelin Bib Gourmand for 9 consecutive years — that alone speaks volumes.
Naturally, my expectations were much higher than usual. As I stood in the queue, a rhythmic chopping sound echoed through the air, accompanied by a lady calling out and taking customers’ orders. As the fast-moving line gradually inched closer, the sounds that had been teasing my ears finally came into full view. From a conversation I couldn’t help but overhear, I gathered that the 2 ladies take turns swapping roles.
What to order at Chai Chuan Tou Yang Rou Tang
Most of the menu items come in 5 sizes, ranging from S$6 to S$10 , so there’s something suitable for every appetite. Just like the local saying goes, “Monkey see, monkey do.” I followed the lead of those queuing ahead of me and ordered the S$8 portion of the 羊杂 (mixed mutton) with a small bowl of Rice (S$0.40) .
For the price, I must say, the portion is pretty generous. There were pieces of mutton, 5 lamb balls, and lamb’s stomach bathed in a light brown soup, garnished with chopped Chinese celery.
The moment the soup hit my tongue, I was greeted by an unusual tingling sensation, accompanied by an almost siap siap mouthfeel. Its robust herbal profile brought to mind a hearty bowl of bak kut teh . It was definitely an acquired taste, and those who dislike herbal flavours may not appreciate it much. As someone who doesn’t mind herbal soups, I still felt that the flavour could be toned down a little to suit a wider audience.
The mutton here has got to be the Wagyu of its kind because, OMG, the meat was so tender that it barely required chewing, There was also no trace of unpleasant gaminess.
The lamb balls were firm yet smooth, and the overall texture reminded me of bouncy fishballs. It also packed a great flavour which wasn’t overly floury.
The stomach pieces were impeccably prepared, with a pleasantly clean flavour and none of that funky offal taste. I even found a couple of pieces of honeycomb tripe.

For chilli lovers, I must say that this one is gentle enough for those who can’t handle too much heat, with a tangy profile reminiscent of the chilli commonly served alongside orh luak .
Who Chai Chuan Tou Yang Rou Tang is best for
It’s perfect for herbal soup lovers who love something comforting for lunch. For those who avoid mutton like the plague because of its potential gaminess, Chai Chuan Tou Yang Rou Tang is a great place to start for its delicious, tender mutton; minus the strong taste.
How to get there?
115 Bukit Merah View Food Centre isn’t exactly near any MRT station. My recommendation would be to alight at Tiong Bahru MRT Station (EW17), get to the Opp Tiong Bahru Stn/Plaza bus stop, and board bus services that take you to Blk 116 .
Do we recommend Chai Chuan Tou Yang Rou Tang ?
If you love robust herbal flavours, then Chai Chuan Tou Yang Rou Tang will be up your alley. Mutton lovers who enjoy innards will appreciate the quality and softness of the lamb here. Oh, and I mustn’t forget the warm, friendly and efficient service here. It’s certainly the cherry on top!

Chinese eateries have taken Singapore by storm lately, introducing us to a wide range of cultures and cuisines, from Yunnan cuisine to traditional Fujian delicacies . Amongst the new wave of restaurants lies Hong Jiu Claypot . Located in Jurong East , they’re all about bold Sichuan flavours.

Image credit: Hong Jiu Claypot
Hong Jiu Claypot is run by a husband-and-wife duo, passionate about serving authentic and high-quality food that embodies Sichuanese cuisine. Leading the kitchen is Chef Wang Yunchang, a Sichuan culinary veteran. With over four decades of experience and having won two national gold awards, it’s safe to say that the food here is in good hands.
Image credit: DAniel Tan via Google Maps
Though our little red dot is no stranger to this cuisine, what makes them stand out is the thought that goes into each dish. Take, for example, their signature 9-Minute Prawn Vermicelli Claypot (price TBD) , where the prawns are handpicked, and the onions are layered to prevent burning.
Alluding to its name, this dish is cooked tableside for exactly nine minutes. Diners get to witness the cooking process up close and personal, right in front of them.
Image credit: Hong Jiu Claypot
Other claypot dishes sound just as yummy as they look, including the Slow-Braised Beef Brisket (price TBD) and Golden Broth Sliced Beef (price TBD) . The former features meaty beef brisket chunks doused in a thick gravy and served with potatoes, while the latter is paired with a lighter, clear broth. Folks who prefer chicken can go for the Braised Chicken (price TBD) claypot instead, which looks equally spicy and flavourful.
Image credit: Hong Jiu Claypot
Their vegetable and side claypots are not one to miss, featuring classics such as Tomato Scrambled Eggs (price TBD) and Hand-Torn Cabbage (price TBD) . The standout here has got to be the Crab Roe Silky Tofu (price TBD) for a more decadent and umami treat.
Image credit: Hong Jiu Claypot
Seafood lovers will be in for a treat, as they also have grilled whole fish. If you can handle spice, the Mala Grilled Fish (price TBD) would definitely bring the heat.Otherwise, the Garlic Grilled Fish (price TBD) is another contender.

Sake Matsuri, which bills itself as Southeast Asia’s largest sake festival, moves to Marina Bay Sands for its 13th edition on Saturday 28 and Sunday 29 November 2026, with regular tickets at S$60 for a three-hour tasting session . The festival takes over Hall C of the Sands Expo and Convention Centre, and tickets are on sale now.
The organiser puts the pour list at more than 500 sakes, shochu and artisanal spirits from over 100 breweries and distilleries. A craft beer festival, Japan HopFest SJ60 Edition, runs alongside on the same weekend.
The move follows a March 2026 edition at the F1 Pit Building and a November 2025 edition at Jewel Changi Airport, beside the Rain Vortex.
Guests at a past Sake Matsuri edition. Photo: Sake Matsuri Singapore
How the sessions work
Each day has two sessions: 11am to 2pm and 4pm to 7pm. The halls close from 2pm to 4pm while the organiser turns them over, so tasting stops completely in that gap.
A regular ticket covers one session only. You cannot stay on into the next one. If you want a longer day, you buy a second session or go VIP. Late arrivals still get in, but the session ends on time, so a 6pm arrival for the 4pm slot gets an hour.
An exhibitor booth at a past edition. Photo: Sake Matsuri Singapore
What a regular ticket gets you
The S$60 regular ticket includes a complimentary Sake Matsuri tasting glass, unlimited sampling across the 500-plus labels and entry to every festival zone, including a dedicated Spirits and Liquor Zone for Japanese gins, whiskies and shochu.
Masterclasses run by sake and shochu educators are included too. Seats are limited and you sign up in person at the Masterclass Lounge on the day. Bottles are on sale at the booths at festival prices.
There is also a food hall. Dishes there are priced separately from the ticket.
Tasting tables at a past edition. Photo: Sake Matsuri Singapore
Bundles and VIP tickets
Groups get bundle pricing on regular tickets: five tickets for S$275, or eight for S$400.
VIP tickets cost S$128 for one person or S$248 for a couple. They cover the full day, both sessions, on your chosen date. On top of everything in the regular ticket, VIP holders get priority for masterclasses, a VIP Lounge for seating through the day and two-day access to Japan HopFest. The lounge stays open during the 2pm to 4pm break, but no food or drinks are served there.
All prices include GST.
A group at the Omu Nomu Craft Sake and Raw Bar booth at a past edition. Photo: Sake Matsuri Singapore
Before you buy
Tickets are final and non-refundable. They can be transferred to someone else if you contact the organiser’s support team at least 48 hours before the event with the new guest’s details.
The organiser strongly recommends buying online in advance and warns that past editions sold out before the festival weekend. Limited tickets might be available at the door.
Alcohol is served only to guests aged 18 and over, and staff can ask for photo ID at registration. Under-18s enter free with an adult but get no wristband or tasting glass. Designated drivers can enter with the ticketed guests they are driving, again without a wristband or glass. Paid parking is available at Marina Bay Sands.
An exhibitor at a past Sake Matsuri edition. Photo: Sake Matsuri Singapore
Details
• What: Sake Matsuri 13th Edition, with Japan HopFest SJ60 Edition alongside (ticketed separately)
• When: Saturday 28 and Sunday 29 November 2026; sessions 11am to 2pm and 4pm to 7pm
• Where: Hall C, Sands Expo and Convention Centre, Marina Bay Sands; nearest MRT is Bayfront (Downtown and Circle lines)
• Price: Regular S$60 per session; five for S$275; eight for S$400; VIP full day S$128, or S$248 for two (GST inclusive)
• Age: Alcohol served to guests 18 and over only

NoMad Singapore, the Orchard Road hotel from the New York brand, has opened reservations for all four of its restaurants and bars, and the first menus are out. The hotel itself is due to open in late 2026, with Hilton yet to name a date.
The four are NoMad Grill and Tropicana Club on level 19, Lù Bar by the pool on level five and Sticky Fingers on the ground floor. The menus mix locally inspired flavours with NoMad classics, from bak kut teh dumplings to a soft-serve take on mango sticky rice. LBRD first looked at NoMad Grill in August , before any menus were out.
Dry-aged rib eye at NoMad Grill. Photo: Hilton
NoMad Grill, the steakhouse on level 19
The flagship is a New York chophouse with in-house dry-ageing and live-fire cooking. The main room seats 65, and a private room takes up to 18 people around one table.
Steaks and chops lead the menu, with a raw bar and a seafood plateau that changes with the season. The local touches are grilled snail toast and fried frog legs with black bean, white pepper and curry leaf. On the seafood side there is wasabi yellowtail crudo, razor clams with escabeche and finger lime, and golden snapper in coconut leche de tigre.
The two big-table dishes are a suckling pig and the return of the NoMad Black Truffle Chicken, both served for two to four people. Dessert is a Baked Alaska, finished at the table.
NoMad Grill runs from breakfast to dinner daily: 6.30am to 10.30am, noon to 3pm and 5.30pm to 10.30pm.
Tropicana Club, cocktails and late nights
The name nods to two clubs: Havana’s Tropicana of 1939 and Singapore’s own Tropicana Club of 1968. This one is a cocktail bar with entertainment, also on level 19.
Cuban classics such as the daiquiri and El Presidente sit next to a long martini list, a pandan vesper and a passion fruit and tomato martini, with no- and low-alcohol versions too. The bar food is where Havana meets Singapore: chilli brown crab empanadas with bottarga aioli, bak kut teh dumplings with shiitake, pork belly and white pepper, and seabream ceviche with calamansi.
It opens 5pm to 1am on Wednesday, Thursday and Sunday, and 5pm to 2am on Friday and Saturday. It is closed on Monday and Tuesday.
Seabream ceviche at Tropicana Club. Photo: Hilton
Sticky Fingers, the soft-serve counter
The 20-seat ground-floor spot changes three times a day. Mornings are coffee from Singapore roaster PPP, house-made viennoiserie and New York-style breakfast sandwiches. Afternoons are soft-serve sundaes, including a Cacio e Pepe Sundae with pecorino, black pepper and olive oil, and the Sticky Mango, which pairs coconut ice cream with vanilla sticky rice and candied peanut. Evenings bring cocktails such as a pandan and coconut Negroni and a banoffee martini. Hours are 8am to 8pm daily.
The Sticky Mango at Sticky Fingers. Photo: Hilton
Lù Bar, by the pool
Lù Bar seats 35 beside the level-five pool, with drinks and small plates including black pepper crab pockets, prawn fresh rolls and a crispy pork belly bánh mì. It opens 9am to 10pm daily.
Prawn fresh rolls at Lù Bar. Photo: Hilton
Booking
Tables at all four go through the NoMad Singapore dining reservations on Hilton’s site. No prices have been published yet for any of the menus. The cocktail list is the work of Leo Robitschek of Sydell Group, a James Beard Award winner for bar programmes, while the food is led by Josh Harnden, a former Eleven Madison Park partner, with Lorenz Hoja, who spent more than ten years with Joël Robuchon, running the Singapore kitchens.

Orang Laut SG , the community group that has sold Southern Islander food mostly through weekend deliveries since 2020, opens its first walk-in cafe on Friday, 23 October, CNA Lifestyle reported. Called Terumbu, it runs at Chef X, #03-103/104 Clarke Quay Central, until 26 December.
Terumbu opens at Chef X on 23 October. Photo: Orang Laut SG
Terumbu is Malay for coral reefs. The pop-up is the 15th residency at Chef X, Far East Organization’s space for home-based and private-dining cooks to run a commercial restaurant for a fixed stint, with a professional kitchen, a dining room for up to 24 and mentoring from chef Isaac Tan of Commonwealth Concepts.
Two savoury dishes and island kueh
The menu is short. The Pulau Bowl is S$15.90 and puts three seafood dishes over jasmine rice with vegetables: asam pedas ikan karang (coral reef fish in a sour, spicy gravy), sotong hitam (squid cooked in its own ink) and sambal udang (stir-fried prawns in sambal).
The sotong hitam uses green-eyed squid, known as sotong nos, which is traditionally caught by line. The family picks it for the amount of ink it carries.
The second dish is bubur lambuk tenggiri, a Spanish mackerel porridge cooked with lemongrass, coconut milk and black pepper. It is S$11.90 with prawns or with squid, and S$13.90 with both.
Bubur lambuk tenggiri is S$11.90 with prawns or squid. Photo: Orang Laut SG
This is not the bubur lambuk handed out at mosques during Ramadan. On the islands it was an everyday dish, made by grinding leftover coral fish, bones and all, at a time when families had no fridge to keep the catch.
Dessert is kueh koleh-koleh and puteri salat, made by a former Pulau Bukom islander. The menu names coral fish without naming the species, because the fish changes with what islander fishermen bring in, including the few bubu (fish trap) makers who still go out to sea.
A family kitchen from Pulau Semakau
Founder Firdaus Sani is a fourth-generation Orang Pulau and Orang Laut whose family lived on Pulau Semakau for generations. They were moved to the mainland in 1977, and the island is now Singapore’s offshore landfill.
His mother does most of the cooking at Terumbu, with his aunt Rohaini running the floor and cousins helping out. The recipes come from his grandmother, Nenek Ninah, and are cooked by feel rather than by measurement.
The family runs Terumbu’s kitchen and floor. Photo: Orang Laut SG
Orang Laut SG started in 2020 as an Instagram page recording the memories, food and traditions of communities moved off the Southern Islands. Terumbu also has a small community gallery on the history of those islands.

Image credit: HANBROTH via Google Maps
Dwaeji-gukbap, AKA Busan-style pork bone soup, is one of Busan’s iconic dishes, its name literally translating to “pork, soup, rice”. It originated during the Korean War in the 1950s, and is made by simmering pork bones for hours, resulting in a milky white broth best served with banchan, or Korean side dishes.
To replicate the flavours you’ll get in Busan, founder Derek Cheong scoured Korea’s best dwaeji-gukbap restaurants to learn more about the dish and bring the techniques back to Singapore. You can see that effort in how the dish is prepared: the broth is boiled for four to eight hours with pork femur bones, pork shank, trotters, pork belly, and pork collar, giving the soup a deep, porky flavour and a creamy, almost gelatinous finish.
Image credit: HANBROTH via Google Maps
Their best-seller is the Original Busan-Style Pork Soup ($9.90) , featuring their signature pork bone soup, served piping hot and packed with tender pork belly and pork collar. Each set also comes with a bowl of steamed rice, kimchi, ssamjang—a spicy Korean chilli sauce—a blend of salt and pepper, and dadaegi, which is a spicy house-made chilli paste.
The recommended way to eat it is to dump the whole bowl of rice into the soup, pao fan style. If you want to zhng up your broth, add a spoonful of the spicy-salty dadaegi paste and the salt-and-pepper blend. Season the pork by dipping it into ssamjang or pairing it with kimchi.
Image credit: HANBROTH via Google Maps
If you’re feeling under the weather, order their Herbal Busan-Style Pork Soup ($11.90) instead, spiked with ginseng, dates, and other Korean herbs for a samgyetang-like experience .
Image credit: HANBROTH via Google Maps
Their Seaweed Busan-style Pork Soup ($11.90) is another variant that’s made by boiling seaweed in the broth, which lends it a deep, umami, and briny taste.
Image credit: HANBROTH via Google Maps
That’s not all: they also have sides to share ‘round the table, including the Potato Pancake ($9.90) : a rosti-like potato pancake drizzled with smoked gochujang-flavoured and bonito-flavoured mayo, then finished with seaweed for additional crunch. The pancake is said to be crispy on the outside, while soft and fluffy on the inside.
Image credit: HANBROTH via Google Maps
Otherwise, their Pork Bossam ($9.90) is also highly popular. It comprises pork shoulder that’s simmered in an aromatic blend of garlic, Korean soybean paste, ginger, and more, served with wasabi, the same salt-and-pepper mix, and ssamjang. Online reviews have raved about it being tender yet not too fatty.
HanBroth is located in Bukit Timah Wet Market & Food Centre , a three-minute walk away from Beauty World MRT Station .
If you’re already in the area, 133 Penang Authentic is worth a visit too, a stall by another award-winning chef in the same hawker centre serving up affordable Penang food. You can also browse our guide to the best foods in Beauty World for more ideas.

What is Telegram?
Telegram is an instant messaging platform which you can download from the App Store and Google Play . Meanwhile, Web Telegram allows you to download the desktop app, or chat directly from your browser if you wish.
The service is free to use and allows seamless communication across your various devices, but they also offer Telegram Premium which is an optional paid subscription.
The top-up unlocks additional features such as faster download speeds, increased limits for file uploads, and more customisation tools like premium stickers, emoji statuses, and animated profile pics. Telegram Premium is priced S$ 7.48 /month . You can get that cost down to S$4.25/month if you purchase an annual subscription at S$ 50.99 .
What are Telegram channels?
Telegram channels are a way for businesses or communities to conveniently broadcast messages to a large audience at the same time. Channels that you join sit in your Chats bar on the Telegram interface so you can get a quick glance at all the updates, and you’ll also be pinged just like with regular messages so you get first dibs on exciting news.
How to join a Telegram channel
On mobile: Open the Telegram channel and press the “Join” button at the bottom of the chat box
On desktop: Open the Telegram channel and press the “Join channel” button at the bottom of the chat box, or on the Channel Info panel on the right.

Watcha Matcha, a new matcha cafe at 15 & 16 Stanley Street, opens on 4 December 2026, and it puts every step of making a cup in front of the customer. The matcha bar in Singapore’s Telok Ayer and Chinatown fringe builds its whole room around water, stone mills and aroma, rather than hiding the process behind the counter.
Image: Watcha Matcha / Buldok Corporation
Watcha Matcha opening date, hours and address
The cafe is at 15 & 16 Stanley Street, Singapore 068734. Doors open to the public on 4 December 2026, with a pre-opening on 3 December. It runs from 10am to 6pm, with last orders at 5pm. Drinks are priced from S$7 to S$12, and non-dairy milk is available for selected drinks.
The team says guests are welcome to book on or after the opening date. Details are on Instagram at @watchamatcha.sg and the brand’s website, watchamatcha.sg.
Image: Watcha Matcha / Buldok Corporation
From water to whisk: how the matcha bar works
The pitch is that a cup of matcha is almost entirely water, so the process starts there. Glass filtration columns at the bar pass water through three mineral layers: tillite stone, muyu stone and hydrogen balls. According to the cafe, tillite brings out sweetness and fresh vegetal notes, while muyu adds umami and body, which supports a dense, velvety foam.
Image: Watcha Matcha / Buldok Corporation
Stone-milled in house, in full view
Matcha loses colour and aroma soon after it is ground, so Watcha Matcha mills its own ceremonial tea leaves on stone mills at the bar. The stones turn slowly and grind without heat, and guests can watch the leaf become powder before it reaches the cup.
Image: Watcha Matcha / Buldok Corporation
Pick your matcha by smell
Instead of one house blend, the cafe offers matcha from three origins, displayed in glass vials and wooden trays at an aroma bar. Guests smell each one and then choose the origin for their Core or Classic Matcha Latte.
• Japan: rich and umami, smooth and refined, with deep umami.
• Korea: fresh and earthy, a clean cup with grassy notes.
• China: bold and nutty, a robust profile with earthy depth.
Image: Watcha Matcha / Buldok Corporation
What is on the Watcha Matcha menu
More than 15 selections are on offer. Drinks are made to order at an open bar following what the cafe calls the Watcha Ritual: sift, whisk, pour, sip.
Image: Watcha Matcha / Buldok Corporation
• Core and Classic: whisked matcha served on its own or layered over milk.
• Nutty lattes: Injeolmi, black sesame, ube and hojicha.
• Fruity lattes: mango, blueberry and strawberry.
• Matcha Clouds: a matcha cream topping over a classic latte, coconut or light sodas such as yuzu and longan osmanthus.
• Pastries and desserts: matcha cheesecake, a fudgy matcha brownie, matcha mochi, sand cookies, matcha and hojicha gelato, and the Crackissant.
Image: Watcha Matcha / Buldok Corporation
The space
Matcha green, brushed metal and raw concrete set the tone, with a long central bar acting as the stage. The stone mills, aroma bar and filtration columns are arranged so every stage of preparation stays visible from the seats.
Image: Watcha Matcha / Buldok Corporation
Our take
Matcha cafes are no longer rare in Singapore. Earlier this month we covered Matchaya’s kakigori promotion in Tiong Bahru , and the category keeps widening. What sets Watcha Matcha apart on paper is the theatre: filtration, milling and aroma selection all happen in view. Whether the cups live up to the show is something we will find out once it opens on 4 December. If you are planning a December cafe crawl, see our things to do this weekend roundup and our Food & Drinks coverage for more openings.

Tucked away in the bustling basement of Golden Mile Food Centre is Charr’d The Hawker , a vibrant Muslim-owned hawker stall run by 2 friendly young chefs. Don’t expect to find wagyu tomahawks at these hawker tables — despite the similar name, this modest Western stall is completely unrelated to Changi’s famous halal steakhouse.
Helmed by 2 young chefs who previously worked in fine-dining kitchens, their dream of running their own F&B business dates all the way back to their university days at The Culinary Institute of America under the Singapore Institute of Technology (SIT). Prior to establishing Charr’d The Hawker, they ran a home-based venture called The Layered Brothers, where they served up lapis rempah , traditional spiced cakes.
Today, they bring expertise picked up from both university and professional kitchens to Golden Mile Food Centre, churning out comfort Western fare.
What to order at Charr’d The Hawker
For my main, I went straight for their bestselling Charr’d Chicken Chop (S$8.50) . It features a crisp chicken chop, a scoop of coleslaw, baked beans, a cup of BBQ sauce, a lightly toasted buttered bun and a choice between garlic butter rice, fries and mashed potato. I opted for the garlic butter rice. Visually, it’s a pretty plate as the colours of the garlic rice and purple cabbage in the coleslaw pop and make it look that much more appetising.
As the stall’s name suggests, I expected nothing less than a perfectly charred protein, and I’m glad to report it delivered. The chicken had a crisp, golden-brown crust that was absolutely delicious and well-seasoned.
The meat didn’t lean as salty as I would have preferred but when dipped in the provided BBQ sauce, it hit all the spots of tangy, spicy and salty. While the sauce was a little watery, I loved how tart it was and how the spice blend lent it a nice warmth.
The chicken fillet was a little thinner than other chicken chops I’ve had in the past, but the crispy skin and seasoning do make up for it.
Although the menu bills it as garlic butter rice, I didn’t pick up much of a garlicky aroma. To me, it tasted a lot more like traditional chicken rice. While it was still tasty, it wasn’t really what I had expected from garlic butter rice.
I appreciated that the rice was cooked nicely — the grains kept a pleasant bite without turning mushy or clumping together.
One of the best elements on the plate for me was the coleslaw. Sporting vibrant orange and purple hues from the shredded carrot and purple cabbage, it was visually appealing. It tasted fresh, helping to cut through the richness of the other components, while its crisp texture added a delightful crunch to every bite. The owner was even kind enough to top up extra coleslaw when I packed up my food to-go after the tasting.
The serving of baked beans was reminiscent of old-school Western hawkers and offered an elevated take on a familiar, old-school staple.

Next, I moved on to the 2-pc Chicken Wing (S$4) . These absolutely stole the spotlight for me, hitting every mark of what a great fried chicken wing should be. Marinated in yoghurt, the meat stayed wonderfully tender and juicy on the inside.
Outside, the crust boasted a super crispy finish packed with savoury seasoning. Honestly, it was a masterclass in fried chicken wings — flavourful enough that you don’t even need the accompanying chilli sauce.
Who is Charr’d The Hawker best for?
If you’re looking for a comforting, old-school Western-style meal with generous and thoughtfully executed sides, Charr’d The Hawker is well worth a visit. The chefs’ fine-dining background shines through in the little details, elevating familiar hawker staples like the vibrant, crunchy coleslaw. It’s an easy go-to for Muslim diners and groups hunting for hearty and affordable Western fare in the Beach Road area.
How to get to Charr’d The Hawker
Charr’d The Hawker is located on the basement level of Golden Mile Food Centre, which is a quick 7-minute walk from Nicoll Highway MRT Station . The station connects to the MRT Circle Line. Take Exit A and walk along Java Road before turning left onto Beach Road.
If you prefer to travel by bus, alight at Opp St. John HQ (01411) or St. John HQ (01419) along Beach Road. Do note that bus service 961M operates exclusively on Sundays and public holidays, while all other bus services operate daily.
Do we recommend Charr’d The Hawker?
Yes! I thoroughly enjoyed every element of the plate as each felt intentional and was done well. That said, on my next visit, I would opt for the chicken wing set instead of the chicken chop. While the chicken chop had a great crust, the fillet was slightly on the thinner side, whereas the wings were easily the star of the meal.

BAO Fast Foods (BFF) is a new concept from London’s cult-favourite BAO . After a homecoming run in Taiwan, the pop-up will next land in Singapore at New Bahru from 11 November 2026 to 28 December 2026 .
But what exactly is this experience that is part fast food joint , part Asian convenience store ? Keep reading to find out more!
Credit: BAO
For those of you who enjoy exploring convenience stores when you’re overseas, especially in Asian countries like Taiwan, you will find the vibes here immaculate. At BFF, there will be a sense of familiarity with a distinct Taiwan flavour.
Credit: BAO
Expect shelves filled with Taiwanese comfort food and snacks , and a rotating selection of grab-and-go items. There will also be self-serve stations and sections featuring BAO’s merchandise .
From protein-packed bites like Egg Sandos and Marinated Eggs to high-fibre sides like “Fried Rice” Quinoa and Golden Kimchi , to sweet treats like Soy Puddings with tiramisu and banoffee toppings, you’ll have plenty to discover and revisit the pop-up for.
Credit: BAO
The signature item, however, is the Chicken Chopper (S$6.50) . Of course, when it comes to Taiwanese snacks, you must have fried chicken . And this is BFF’s take on the classic street food, perfected over 140 iterations.
You will notice that the chicken is cut with the bone left in place as a handle, making it easy to eat. By dipping the chicken in a soymilk batter and coating it in a tapioca starch mix, BFF ensures the meat stays juicy while having a light, crackly crust on the outside.
Flavours to look forward to include Original Crispy , Flame Glazed , and Master Scalded . The first is seasoned with Taiwanese white pepper, the second is flavoured with soy-garlic or mala hot honey glaze, and the third is dipped in a boiling soy-based master sauce with star anise and cinnamon.
Credit: BAO
For a more filling meal, you can order the Chicken Chopper as part of a rice box (S$7.95) , or pair it with Dan Dan Noodles (S$6.50) or Beef Cup Noodle (S$12.50) . Combos from S$9.50 are also available.
Credit: BAO
Another staple of Taiwanese food culture is tea ! And you will be able to find a selection of Taiwanese craft tea here at the BFF pop-up. Highlights include the nitro-infused Fluffy Natural Alishan Wintermelon (S$5.95) , the carbonated Orange Guava Beauty Tea (S$6.50) , and the rich Original Peanut Oatside Milk (S$6) .
If anything about this pop-up excites you, mark your calendars from 11 November to 28 December. It’s time to have a date at the convenience store!

World Christmas Market returns from 10 December 2026
Image credit: World Christmas Market
PSA: The Christmas market that drew more than 218,000 people to Marina Bay last year is moving house. World Christmas Market is back for a third edition, now called A Christmas Story by World Christmas Market . It runs from 10 December 2026 to 3 January 2027 on the grounds of METT Hotel Singapore and Fort Canning Park . Even better, entry is free for everyone.
We Visited World Christmas Market 2025, A Festive Fair At Bayfront With Over 40 Stalls
The fair started in 2024 at The Promontory at Marina Bay. In 2025, it moved to the much bigger Bayfront Event Space as Togetherland by World Christmas Market .
We went last year and counted over 40 food and drink stalls, from Rollney’s ice cream-stuffed chimney cakes to chilled and grilled oysters at Slurp Your Oysters.
Image credit: World Christmas Market
This year the organisers, DareDreamer, are swapping the waterfront for something greener and more old-school, with the fair spread across the hilltop park and the grounds of the colonial-era hotel.
The fair is split into three zones. The first, The Story Terrace, has festive shopping, gifts, and hands-on workshops. It’s also home to The Long Table, a communal dining setup where you can share a meal with friends or end up chatting with strangers.
Image credit: World Christmas Market
Next is The Piazza, the main square. A 38-foot real Christmas tree stands in the middle, with smaller decorated trees all around it. The third zone, The Merry Grounds, is where the food is. Expect seasonal bites, festive drinks, and plenty of reasons to stick around. If you’re mainly going to eat, start here. The full vendor lineup is still TBD, since the festival is still taking applications from F&B, retail, and craft vendors. We’ll update this article once the stalls are confirmed.
Across the grounds, look out for giant nutcrackers and glowing reindeer, which make good photo backdrops. There’s plenty of music too. A 42-piece orchestra plays on opening weekend. Brass sextets, saxophone quartets, and choirs perform on other dates throughout the season.
Image credit: World Christmas Market
On opening night, 10 December 2026, the gates open at 5pm. The tree-lighting and opening ceremony starts at 7.30pm, so arrive early for a good spot. The fair also stays open until 1am on Christmas Eve and New Year’s Eve, so it works for a late-night date or a countdown with friends.
